egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-ma.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat, made with butter

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat is made from eggs, a small amount of butter, and diced cooked meat (such as ham, bacon, or chicken). The dish is usually served hot for breakfast or a light dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs provide all essential amino acids.
Butter gives the dish a distinctive aroma and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.
Meat adds extra protein and makes the meal more filling.
The “scrambled” technique yields a softer, creamier texture than a traditional folded omelet.
The dish is popular in many cuisines, from American breakfasts to European plates.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Eggs contain B2, B12 and folate, while meat provides niacin and pyridoxine, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vitamin D content
items.content: Butter and egg yolks are natural sources of vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium from eggs and zinc from meat help maintain a healthy immune system.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of fats, proteins, and a small amount of carbs offers lasting satiety.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Butter is rich in saturated fat, so consume in moderation if you have cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should monitor portion size.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use fresh, safe-to-eat meat to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Melt butter in a skillet, pour lightly beaten eggs, add diced meat, and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly until the mixture thickens but remains tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours and reheat in a pan or microwave.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-made.title: Egg White Omelet, Scrambled or Fried with Oil

content.title: About
content.content: An egg white omelet is made from the clear liquid of eggs, cooked on a skillet with a small amount of vegetable oil. Egg whites are high in protein and contain virtually no fat, making this dish popular in low‑calorie diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is composed mainly of water and proteins, especially albumin.
Cooking with oil gives the omelet a softer texture compared to dry cooking.
Egg whites contain no cholesterol, unlike the yolk.
Protein‑rich egg white omelets are a staple in sports nutrition for quick protein replenishment.
Whipping the whites before cooking creates a fluffier, scramble‑like consistency.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Egg whites provide about 10–12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Pure egg white contains almost no fat, suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3), which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium in egg whites contributes to the body’s antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Very low in carbs
items.content: Egg white omelet has negligible carbohydrates, fitting well into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High‑heat by‑products
items.content: Excessive heating can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

items.title: Lack of vitamins D and A
items.content: Unlike yolk, egg whites contain virtually no vitamin D or A, so prolonged exclusive use may lead to deficiencies.

items.title: Sodium from oil
items.content: Using heavily salted oil can increase the sodium content of the dish.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Whisk egg whites with a pinch of salt, heat 1‑2 tsp of vegetable oil in a skillet, pour the mixture, and cook 2‑3 minutes until lightly golden. For scrambled style, continuously stir until the whites set but remain tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. It can be frozen for up to 1 month if cut into portion‑size pieces.
